name: PT Transcoal Pacific Tbk

frontmatter.title: Transcoal Pacific: a solid barge franchise inside a concentrated float
frontmatter.summary: Transcoal Pacific moves coal, nickel and palm oil on its own tug-and-barge fleet, with 100 tugs, 90 barges and 5.4% of national coal output. The operating business is sound and modestly growing; the shares are not cheap. At Rp1,780 the stock trades at 38.9x FY2026E earnings and 4.7x today's fundamental value. We rate SELL with a Rp1,196 target.
thesis: Volume-led franchise: 42.6Mt moved in FY2025 and a 46.2Mt company plan for 2026, with nickel and palm-oil cargo diversifying the mix away from coal.
Cash earnings are stronger than the data pack shows: restating D&A from the LK lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR640.2bn and cuts ND/EBITDA to 1.8x.
The capex peak is now: the newbuild tug and barge programme drives capex to 30.0% of revenue in 2026, then normalises toward replacement levels.
Still expensive: 38.9x FY2026E P/E, 12.7x EV/EBITDA and 3.9x P/BV price in growth the fleet cannot deliver on our volume path.
Konglo lens: the 4.7x fundamental-value premium only partly compresses in twelve months, so our SELL target sits above fair value.

catalysts.event: HSC-designated shares, which include TCPI, leave the IHSG calculation
ESDM Minerba Convex opens RKAB consultation and permitting clinics
Free float must reach the next regulatory step; controller sell-down or new shares
MSCI decision on Indonesia's Standalone status
FY2026 audited results and the 2027 volume and capex plan

blocks.text: Transcoal Pacific is an independent Indonesian owner-operator of tugboats, barges and mother vessels that carries coal, nickel ore, industrial diesel and palm oil, plus transhipment and assist-tug services [S2 p.34]. It is a real operating franchise: 100 tugs and 90 barges, a 5.4% share of national coal production moved, and long-term nickel contracts signed in 2025 [S2 p.10, p.35, p.85]. The equity story is different. The shares changed hands at Rp1,780 after falling from a twelve-month peak of Rp13,525, and even there they trade at 38.9x forward earnings and 12.7x EV/EBITDA [S0].

Our view is that the operating business is worth roughly Rp417 per share on a twelve-month fundamental basis, against Rp1,780 today. The gap is a float phenomenon rather than an operating one: the controlling shareholders hold 80.0% of the shares [S2 p.34], the free float is 13.77% in the exchange's IDX-IC mirror dated 27 October 2026 [S0], and TCPI sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which removes it from the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S9; S12]. The konglo lens therefore keeps only part of the premium for twelve months, giving a Rp1,196 target and a -32.1% expected return; hence SELL [S0].

What moves the value: the volume and tariff path after the 2026 company plan, the capex tail from the newbuild programme, and the regime calendar (the free-float step and the MSCI decision). The first is modelled from the company's own IDR2,201.0bn revenue projection; the second is the main reason our DCF value of Rp303 sits below the multiple-based cross-checks [S2 p.84].

The company provides sea transportation for coal, nickel, other bulk cargo, industrial diesel and crude palm oil, plus transhipment, assist-tug rental, floating-barge fuel storage and mining-support services [S2 p.34], and the company lists the same service lines on its website [S6]. Coal still dominates cargo volume, but nickel ore has become a growing contributor and the company is extending into FAME and other energy-transition cargoes [S2 p.25, p.155]. Revenue is overwhelmingly voyage-charter and contract freight rather than owned-asset leasing, so utilisation and tariff per tonne are the operating levers [S2 p.35].

The fleet at end-2025 comprised 100 tugs, 90 barges, 6 mother vessels, six floating cranes, seven sea trucks and ancillary heavy equipment, owned directly and supplemented by chartered-in capacity from shipping partners [S2 p.35]. That mix lets the company flex capacity to voyage-charter demand rather than carry fixed hire through a trough [S2 p.35]. Operations are concentrated where the coal and nickel are: Sangatta and Bengalon in East Kalimantan, Asam Asam in South Kalimantan, Wolo, Pomalaa, Morosi and Morowali in Sulawesi, and Weda and Obi in North Maluku [S2 p.35].

The commercial strategy is to secure medium- and long-term contracts for base-load volume while running hundreds of spot voyage charters around them [S2 p.10, p.26]. In 2025 the company signed two five-year nickel-ore transportation agreements with a Southeast Sulawesi miner, one using tug-and-barge and one using bulk carriers, both with a five-year extension option, plus a one-year assist-tug extension with a major South Kalimantan coal miner [S2 p.10]. Capital spending follows the contracts: the newbuild tug order placed in 2025 and the additional barge added in October are the current capex phase [S2 p.12-13].

Transcoal is a subsidiary of PT Sari Nusantara Gemilang, which holds the controlling stake alongside PT Karya Permata Insani, while the public holds the remainder per the annual report and the exchange mirror puts the free float at 13.77% [S2 p.34; S0]. The group structure runs through PT Kanz Gemilang Utama, which owns PT Sentra Makmur Lines and PT Energy Transporter Indonesia [S5]. With 101 employees the company is a lean operator relative to the revenue it moves [S0].

Revenue is not split by commodity in the summary disclosure, but coal dominates cargo and nickel is the deliberate growth leg: management describes nickel ore as a growing contributor and is adding FAME and other energy-transition products to the mix [S2 p.25, p.155]. The 2025 contract book pairs two five-year nickel-ore agreements and a one-year assist-tug extension with hundreds of voyage charters, a blend that gives base-load visibility without locking the fleet to a single tariff [S2 p.10, p.26]. The stated priorities are fleet reliability, operational efficiency and securing medium- to long-term cargo, which is the right posture for a business whose revenue fell in 2025 on tariffs while volume rose [S2 p.20, p.78].

Capital intensity is the defining feature. The fleet is carried at revalued cost for vessels and depreciated over useful lives of up to two decades, and annual depreciation is IDR366.0bn [S2 p.251-252, p.269]. The newbuild programme is funded with operating cash flow and bank facilities signed with state-owned banks during 2025, so capex rather than demand is the near-term cash-flow swing factor [S2 p.13; S3 p.10]. That is why we model the company as an asset-heavy operator that must reinvest to stand still, not as an asset-light freight forwarder.

Within the domestic chain Transcoal is a scale challenger: it moved 5.4% of national coal output, holds a fleet few independents can match, and operates in the main Kalimantan and Sulawesi loading areas [S2 p.35, p.85]. Its customer list includes major miners such as Kaltim Prima Coal and Arutmin, and its safety record has been recognised by both [S2 p.12]. The company is not integrated into mining or trading; it sells freight capacity, so its fortunes track miners' output plans and the freight cycle rather than the coal price itself [S2 p.34].

Indonesian coal production reached about 790Mt in 2025, ahead of the government's production target, and coal remains the backbone of domestic bulk shipping demand [S2 p.25]. The house coal driver deck prices Newcastle at US$150/t spot, US$118/t for FY2027E and US$105/t long term, while HBA is US$127/t spot against US$112/t for FY2027E; for a logistics operator the level matters less than the direction of trade volumes and tariffs [S2 p.25]. A flat-to-lower coal price with stable Indonesian output is the base case [S2 p.25].

Policy supports the domestic fleet. The Domestic Market Obligation, nickel downstreaming and the cabotage principle keep Indonesian-flagged operators inside the coal and nickel chain [S2 p.25]. The ESDM continues to run the RKAB work-plan and budget approval cycle [S4], with a consultation clinic at Minerba Convex in early November 2026 that determines miners' permitted output and therefore cargo availability [S7]. The risk on the other side is supply of shipping capacity: additional fleet and new entrants have intensified competition and pressured tariffs and margins [S2 p.25].

Transcoal moved 5.4% of national coal production in 2025, down from its prior-year share, so it is a leading independent challenger rather than a price-setter [S2 p.85]. Its moat is the combination of a large owned fleet, multi-year contracts with major miners, a safety record recognised by Arutmin and Kaltim Prima Coal, and the operating knowledge of specific river and anchorage systems [S2 p.12]. Those assets are real but replicable with capital, which is why the industry earns a competitive return rather than a monopoly one [S2 p.25].

Five forces are mixed. Buyer concentration is high because a handful of coal miners dominate cargo, but contracts are multi-year and switching mid-contract is costly [S2 p.10]. Supplier power sits with shipyards and fuel suppliers, and fuel-price volatility is a named cost risk [S2 p.20]. Substitutes such as rail and conveyor are limited for the island-to-mother-vessel leg, while new entrants can add barges quickly [S2 p.25]. Rivalry is the binding force, and it is why the company's own 2025 revenue fell while volume rose: the average freight rate declined [S2 p.78].

The demand engine is national output. Indonesian coal production is around 790Mt, with the government's target cleared, and the company carries 5.4% of that volume [S2 p.25, p.85]. Growth in the next cycle depends on two things: whether miners' RKAB approvals allow output to rise, and whether nickel and FAME cargoes scale fast enough to offset a plateau in thermal coal [S2 p.25, p.155; S7]. The ESDM's permitting cycle is therefore a direct volume signal for this business, not a distant policy abstraction [S7].

Regulation cuts both ways. DMO, cabotage and domestic-processing rules protect the Indonesian-flagged fleet from foreign competition, while tightening environmental and vessel-certification requirements raise compliance cost [S2 p.20, p.25]. The 2026 regime adds a capital-markets layer: HSC status [S9; S12], the higher free-float requirement [S13; S0] and the MSCI consultation [S11] are not shipping rules, but they set the discount at which the equity trades relative to the fleet's cash flows. A reader should keep the operating and regime layers separate, because they move on different calendars.

External influences are fuel, FX, weather and the coal cycle. Fuel-price volatility and unpredictable weather are explicitly named as risks to continuity and cost structure, and revenue is in rupiah while bunker fuel is dollar-linked, so the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD is a real margin variable [S2 p.20]. The coal deck's Newcastle path of US$118/t for FY2027E, against US$150/t spot, is the reference we use for trade volumes rather than for the company's own tariff [S2 p.25]. None of these is a reason to own or avoid the shares on its own; together they explain why the freight cycle is shallower than the coal-price cycle.

The competitive landscape is fragmented at the small end and concentrated at the large end. Transcoal, with its owned fleet and multi-year contracts, sits in the large independent tier alongside a handful of listed and family-owned operators, while hundreds of small barge owners compete for spot voyage charters [S2 p.10, p.35]. That structure supports a base-load contract business but caps pricing power in the spot market, which is exactly the mix the 2025 results show: volume up, tariff down, gross margin broadly stable [S2 p.28, p.78].

FY2025 revenue was IDR1,914.3bn, down -0.6% on the prior year, because the average transportation tariff fell even as volume rose to 42.6Mt from 42.0Mt [S2 p.28, p.78]. Gross profit was IDR459.8bn and gross margin held at 24.0%, broadly in line with 2024 [S2 p.6]. Operating expenses rose to IDR185.7bn on higher transportation and vessel-certification costs tied to the larger cargo base [S2 p.78].

The important correction to the data pack is depreciation. The LK note shows total depreciation of IDR366.0bn in FY2025 and IDR362.5bn in FY2024, not the small fractions the direct-method cash flow implies [S2 p.269]. Restating D&A lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR640.2bn and an EBITDA margin of 33.4%, which is consistent with the annual report's own EBITDA line [S2 p.6]. On that basis net debt of IDR1,129.2bn is 1.76 times EBITDA, comfortable for a fleet operator [S0].

The nine months to 30 September 2026 show the operating leverage: revenue of IDR1,634.8bn and profit before tax of IDR213.4bn, both well ahead of the comparable 2025 period [S3 p.7]. Gross margin improved to 25.0% on lower fuel and charter costs [S3 p.7]. The company's own 2026 plan is revenue of IDR2,201.0bn, profit of IDR195.0bn and volume of 46.2Mt, which we adopt as the base for FY2026E [S2 p.84].

The gross-margin input is stated at the FY2025 fuel base, so the fuel link adds to cost when the deck's Brent path is above that base; after the link the FY2026E effective margin is 25.0%, matching the nine-month LK, and it eases toward 24.0% as tariff competition offsets volume growth [S2 p.25; S3 p.7]. Our forecast has revenue growing 15.0% in FY2026E to IDR2,201.4bn and then decelerating to 5.5% and below [S2 p.25]. EBITDA rises to IDR803.6bn, but free cash flow to the firm is IDR69.7bn because capex peaks at 30.0% of revenue; it rises to IDR160.2bn in FY2027E as the newbuild programme completes. Capex is the swing factor: IDR617.7bn in FY2025 and IDR660.4bn in FY2026E, then a normalisation toward replacement spending [S0; S3 p.10].

The tax line is the other correction. The shipping final tax is deducted above the reported profit line, so applying the reported tax rate to a profit that already nets it out double-counts the burden; the model instead carries the 15.8% combined rate implied by the final tax plus the corporate charge at the forecast margin, below the FY2025 burden because the fixed final tax dilutes as profit rises [S2 p.227; S3 p.7]. We rebuild FY2026E on that structure: the final tax is about one and three-quarter per cent of revenue and the corporate charge is small, so FY2026E net profit to parent reaches IDR228.6bn, above the IDR195.0bn company plan and above the nine-month parent actual of IDR202.7bn [S2 p.84, p.227; S3 p.7, p.8]. There is no Q4 one-off absorbing the gap; the earlier model carried too much opex and too high a tax rate, and both are corrected here.

Capital allocation is dividend plus growth: DPS of 13.7 at a payout of 27.8%, while retaining enough to fund the fleet [S0]. The earnings-quality screen is clean on accruals: operating cash flow has run ahead of net profit, receivables fell in 2025, there is no inventory build, and the auditor issued an unqualified opinion [S0; S2 p.76]. The main quality caveat is the final shipping tax booked below the operating line, which we now reflect explicitly in the effective rate rather than understating the burden [S2 p.227].

The multi-year record shows a business that grew through the post-COVID coal boom and then flattened: revenue moved from IDR1,758.1bn in FY2022A to IDR1,825.6bn and IDR1,926.1bn before easing to IDR1,914.3bn, while EBIT peaked at IDR353.9bn and fell to IDR274.1bn as tariffs compressed [S0]. The balance sheet carries the fleet: property and equipment of IDR2,951.1bn, debt of IDR1,195.7bn and equity of IDR2,065.0bn [S0]. That is a leverage ratio the company can service at current EBITDA, but it leaves little room for a second capex cycle without new borrowing.

Working capital is a modest drag rather than a red flag: operating working capital was IDR361.6bn, and receivables fell year-on-year while revenue was flat, which is the opposite of the classic channel-stuffing pattern [S0]. Capex has run above depreciation for three years — IDR702.6bn, IDR681.8bn and IDR617.7bn against depreciation restated at IDR366.0bn — which is consistent with fleet rejuvenation rather than maintenance catch-up [S0; S2 p.269]. The funding gap has been met with bank debt, lifting net debt to IDR1,129.2bn [S0].

On our forecasts, revenue reaches IDR2,322.5bn in FY2027E and EBITDA IDR826.7bn, with net debt easing to IDR1,178.9bn as capex normalises and free cash flow turns positive [S0]. Return on equity rises from 5.7% to 9.4%, still a modest return on a capital-heavy base [S0]. The forecast assumes no tariff recovery: the company holds its volume plan and earns back its cost of capital only when the capex tail rolls off, which is the most likely path given the contract book [S2 p.10, p.84].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because a barge fleet is a finite-life, capital-intensive asset whose value depends on the capex required to keep it earning, not on a single year's multiple [S2 p.269]. EV/EBITDA and P/BV are the cross-checks. The cost of equity is 13.3%, built as (risk-free 7.4% minus the default spread 1.6%) plus a levered beta of 1.11 times the sum of the mature-market ERP 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%. Pre-tax debt is priced at 9.4%, and the debt weight 12.4% is market-value D/(D+E) at today's price; WACC is 12.5% [S0]. The beta is the industry-default unlevered beta relevered for the market-value debt/equity ratio, not a company regression, and the report says so [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR2,838.8bn and Rp303 per share after net debt and minorities, with 45.8% of value in the terminal period [S0]. The capex path is what keeps this below the market: the fleet earns an operating return, but the reinvestment needed to sustain it consumes most of the cash in the near term [S3 p.10].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp422 per share at 5.4x restated FY2025A EBITDA of IDR640.2bn, 38.9% above the primary method [S0]. The peer set is the like-for-like coal-barging and coal-logistics group — MAHA, MBSS, PSAT, PSSI and CNKO — not the all-industry COAL_LOGISTICS list, which mixes traders and high-multiple outliers such as SGER, BESS and ALII; the observations and medians are in the peer table. On this set the EV/EBITDA median is 5.4x and the P/B median is 1.1x, so the cross-checks sit above the DCF but far below the all-industry multiple that previously flattered the blend [S0].
The P/BV check gives Rp460 at 1.1x book, 51.5% above the DCF, because the book is a depreciated fleet rather than a marked-to-market one [S0].

The bridge is built from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet in the data pack, not the 30 September interim; the twelve-month roll applies the cost of equity but does not debit the incremental net debt from the remaining capex, so the target is modestly optimistic on that line, and the 9M2026 investing outflow already matches the full-year capex plan with Q4 delivery risk [S3 p.10; S0]. Blending the three at the house weights gives a fundamental value of Rp370 per share today and Rp417 on a twelve-month forward basis [S0]. At Rp1,780 the shares trade at 4.7 times today's fundamental value. The lens then keeps part of that premium for twelve months: with the HSC flag [S9; S12] and the free-float step due within 4.9 months [S13; S0], the base regime case closes 40% of the log gap and targets Rp1,053; the bear and bull regime cases give Rp568 and Rp2,108 [S9; S13; S11]. The probability-weighted lens produces the Rp1,196 target, a -32.1% expected total return, hence SELL [S0].

The reverse DCF makes the same point from the other side: today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of about 28.5%, against our 5.5% [S0]. Nothing in the 2026 plan or the coal deck supports that acceleration; it is a float premium, not a growth forecast [S2 p.84; S0]. The smallest plausible change to the capex path or the coal deck would move the DCF more than a change in the multiple, which is why we anchor on it.

The largest risk is regime, not operations. TCPI is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S9; S12], leaves the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S12], and must lift its free float from 13.77% to 15.0% by 31 March 2027 under the rule in force from 31 March 2026 that sets an interim step for names in its free-float band [S13; S0], a gap of 1.23 percentage points of 5,000m shares. A controller sell-down or a new share issue would fix the float but can pressure the price; the gap is a small fraction of market cap and a few days of ADTV, so a modest placement could close it. MSCI's Standalone consultation, with a decision by 30 June 2027, is a second dated overhang [S11]. Likelihood is high and the impact on the multiple is high. If the premium closed all the way to fundamental value, the shares would be worth Rp417 on a twelve-month basis; that full-convergence path sits outside the house lens, which deliberately does not assume instant convergence, but it is the downside the lens does not carry [S0].

Contract duration is shorter than asset life. The nickel contracts run five years with a five-year option and the assist-tug extension is one year, while the fleet depreciates over up to two decades; the first 2027-30 renewal at lower tariffs is therefore the main terminal-value downside, and the decelerating revenue and margin path modelled here is the step-down we carry rather than terminal re-contracting at today's rates [S2 p.10, p.25].

The commodity risk is second-order but real. The coal deck carries Newcastle at US$118/t for FY2027E against US$150/t spot; a weaker coal price would trim miners' output plans and with them cargo demand and tariffs [S2 p.25]. Operating risks are weather disruption, delivery delays on the newbuild tugs and accidents, any of which would hit utilisation and the contract timetable [S2 p.20]. Fuel and FX are part-managed: Brent is carried at US$84.0/bbl and the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD. Our estimate that fuel is a modest share of cost of revenues and that half of a move is passed through voyage-charter rates is an analyst assumption, not a company disclosure; the annual report names fuel only as a cost risk [S2 p.20]. Across a wide range of fuel shares and pass-through assumptions the base-case EBITDA effect is an order of magnitude below the capex sensitivity, because no fuel shock enters the base; the assumption and its arithmetic are disclosed in the model's basis.

Governance and liquidity risks sit alongside the regime risk. The controlling shareholders hold 80.0% [S2 p.34], related-party balances are present [S3 p.5], and the controlling shareholders' capital-markets agenda can change the share count or the asset mix. Against that, daily traded value of IDR11.2bn is adequate for the position sizes this name supports, and the auditor is a reputable firm with an unqualified opinion [S0; S2 p.76].

Our business scenarios are mirrored: the bear case subtracts a fixed amount from revenue growth and from gross margin, the bull case adds the same, and probabilities are 50%, 25% and 25% for base, bear and bull [S0]. The konglo regime scenarios are separate and described in the governance section. Signposts that would change the view: a free-float resolution that removes the overhang, a tariff recovery visible in quarterly revenue per tonne, new nickel or FAME contracts that lift volume above the 46.2Mt plan, and capex discipline once the newbuilds are delivered [S2 p.10, p.84].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Sari Nusantara Gemilang is the controlling shareholder, PT Karya Permata Insani holds a further stake and the public holds the balance in the annual report's table [S2 p.34], while the exchange mirror shows insider holdings of 80.0% and a free float of 13.77% [S0]. The group runs through PT Kanz Gemilang Utama, which owns PT Sentra Makmur Lines and PT Energy Transporter Indonesia, and the related-party payable is a reminder that the controlling shareholders' other vehicles are counterparties [S5; S3 p.5]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the annual report, and the company had no outstanding bonds at end-2025 [S2 p.11].

Governance basics are adequate for an IDX mid-cap: the board includes an independent commissioner unaffiliated with the controlling shareholders, the FY2025 accounts were audited by Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan & Rekan with an unqualified opinion, and the dividend record is continuous, with Rp6.5 paid over the trailing twelve months [S2 p.49, p.76; S0]. The structure flags are the konglo ones rather than accounting ones: HSC status [S9; S12], the pending free-float step [S13; S0], and the risk that a group corporate action dilutes minorities.

The konglo lens is the bridge between the operating value and the price. At Rp1,780 the shares are 4.7 times the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp417; the HSC flag and the free-float deadline each add to the share of the gap the lens assumes is kept, so the base case closes only 40% of the log gap and targets Rp1,053, with Rp1,196 after weighting [S9; S12; S13; S0]. In plain terms, a rich float-driven price can stay rich for a year even as operating value says otherwise, and the target reflects that persistence rather than a forecast that the premium disappears immediately.

The overlay's registry-derived statements are archived and dated: the HSC list as of 22 October 2026 naming TCPI [S9; S12], the free-float rule in force from 31 March 2026 with the 15.0% step for the applicable tier by 31 March 2027 [S13], the MSCI consultation opened on 15 October 2026 with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S11], and the free float of 13.77% in the exchange's IDX-IC mirror dated 27 October 2026 [S0]. TCPI is HSC-listed but is not a member of any of the registry's family conglomerate groups; the lens applies because the house definition covers HSC names, and the report describes it as HSC-listed rather than as a family conglomerate [S9; S12].

On ESG, the company's main exposures are marine fuel emissions, spill risk and crew safety. It reports TBT-free anti-fouling coatings across the fleet, energy-efficiency and fuel-monitoring systems, and safety awards from Arutmin and Kaltim Prima Coal, while the cargo mix is shifting toward nickel and FAME, which are less coal-carbon-intensive [S2 p.12, p.27, p.155].

The regime calendar is the nearest set of catalysts. HSC shares leave the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S9; S12], the free-float step falls due on 31 March 2027 [S13; S0], and MSCI decides on Standalone status by 30 June 2027 [S11]. On the operating side, the ESDM's RKAB consultation at Minerba Convex in early November 2026 determines miners' permitted output for the coming cycle and therefore cargo availability [S7]. The FY2026 audited results and the 2027 plan, expected around March, will show whether the 46.2Mt volume plan and the capex normalisation are on track [S2 p.84].

Between updates we watch five KPIs: cargo volume against the 46.2Mt plan, revenue per tonne as the tariff indicator, gross margin against the 25.0% plan level, capex against the 30.0% budget, and net debt to EBITDA, currently 1.8x [S0; S2 p.84]. On the regime side we track the free float, any controller sell-down or new issue, and index decisions [S13; S0]. A tariff recovery or a float resolution that removes the overhang would be the two developments most likely to make us revisit the SELL stance [S0].

bear.narrative: Chinese and Indian coal imports soften while new barge capacity keeps tariffs falling; the 2027 free-float step and HSC exclusion keep a structural discount on the shares.

bull.narrative: Nickel-ore and FAME contracts ramp, fleet utilisation tightens as marginal operators exit, freight tariffs recover with a coal-price rebound toward the deck's spot levels, and the 2027 capex roll-off de-levers the balance sheet faster than the base case assumes.

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]
free float 13.77% must reach 15.0% by 2027-03-31 — controller sell-down or new shares inside the window [konglo deck S25]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +15.0% is the company's own 2026 projection (revenue Rp2,201.0bn vs Rp1,914.3bn 2025) on 46.23Mt volume, +8.6% [S2 p.84]. Thereafter volume grows ~4-5% with national coal output near 790Mt and tariff competition from new fleet capacity capping rate gains [S2 p.25]; coal deck newc FY2027E 118.0 vs spot 150.35 implies no price tailwind.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 2025 gross margin was 24.0% [S2 p.6] and 9M2026 rose to 25.0% [S3 p.7] on lower fuel and charter costs. This input is stated at the FY2025 fuel base; the 15% fuel link with 50% pass-through adds about 3pp to COGS at the FY2026E Brent deck, so the FY2026E input is set at 27.2% to reproduce the 25.0% effective gross margin the 9M LK reports. The effective margin then eases to 24.0% as new entrants pressure tariffs [S2 p.25]; no default haircut below the last actual.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal price is not a direct COGS line for a barging fleet: the LK cost note and MD&A name fuel, charters, crew and repairs as cost drivers, not coal [S2 p.20, p.78]. Coal affects demand and freight rates, captured in revenue_growth, so no COGS share is assigned.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: No coal-indexed cost line exists, so there is nothing to pass through; the coal channel is modelled entirely through cargo volume and freight-rate growth in revenue_growth [S2 p.78].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel is a named external cost driver of the business [S2 p.20], but the company does not disclose a cost share. The 15% is our analyst assumption for the tug-and-barge mix, not a sourced fact; half is assumed recovered through rate adjustments. The report labels it an estimate and tests 10-25% share with 0-100% pass-through in section 5.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Analyst assumption, not a company disclosure: voyage-charter tariffs are assumed to carry fuel-adjustment clauses and to reprice at each fixture, so half of a Brent move is recovered in freight rates rather than lost to margin [S2 p.20 for fuel as a named risk only].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 was 9.7% of revenue [S2 p.6]; 9M2026 fell to 6.8% as revenue grew against near-flat absolute opex [S3 p.7]. We calibrate FY2026E to 7.5%, between the 9M actual and the full-year 2025 rate, then let it drift up to 9.0% as certification and crew costs normalise.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is restated from the LK note to Rp366.0bn (19.1% of revenue) in 2025 [S2 p.269], not the Rp17.4bn in the data pack. Held at 19% while the newbuild programme depreciates, easing to 17.5% long term as older units are fully written down.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Fleet rejuvenation is live: 16 tugboats ordered April 2025 and two more September 2025 plus a new barge October 2025 [S2 p.12-13], and 9M2026 investing outflow was Rp662.8bn [S3 p.10]. Capex stays near 30% of revenue in 2026, then normalises toward replacement level: terminal capex is set to 1.1x D&A (0.175 D&A share), so the fleet is not assumed to shrink.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 18.9% of revenue [S0]; the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet shows 13.5% after receivable collection [S0 latest_bs]. We use 17%, between the two.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Tax is the shipping final tax plus corporate tax on non-shipping profit. FY2025 shows Rp33.559bn final tax and Rp3.164bn corporate tax on pre-final-tax profit of Rp162.150bn, a 22.6% combined burden [S2 p.227]; 9M2026 shows Rp29.147bn final tax and Rp3.099bn corporate tax on pre-final-tax profit of Rp242.522bn, a 13.3% combined burden as the fixed final tax dilutes with margin [S3 p.7]. We rebuild the forecast on that structure: the final tax is about 1.78% of revenue, the corporate charge about 2.4% of post-final-tax profit, and the combined rate on the model's pre-final PBT is 15.8% in FY2026E, rising to 17.9% as margins compress. The 28.5% figure divides by PBT that already deducts the final tax and is not the rate to apply. The engine has one tax line, so the structure is proxied by this combined rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense was 9.7% of opening debt [S0]; 9M2026 interest of Rp67.0bn on ~Rp1.2tr debt annualises to ~7.2% [S3 p.7], consistent with BI-rate cuts to 5.75% [macro deck].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default 2.6%; cash balances are small relative to debt so this is not a value driver [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 showed Rp117bn net bank-loan drawdown to fund the fleet programme (proceeds Rp373bn less repayments Rp256bn) [S3 p.10]; borrowing tapers as capex normalises.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other non-operating items were a net Rp49.9bn charge, dominated by the shipping final tax of Rp33.6bn that is captured in tax_rate; the residual (bank charges, tax penalties, FX) is not recurring and is set to zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 6.7% of FY2025 net profit and 7.6% of 9M2026 PBT through the 14.5% ETI and 1% SML stakes; we use 5% as earnings mix shifts to wholly owned operations.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp6.5 on EPS of Rp23.4 is a 27.8% payout [S0]; the 2026 GMS paid Rp32.5bn [S3 p.10]. Policy is GMS-determined, so we hold 30%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No splits, rights issues or buybacks; 5,000m shares outstanding [S2 p.34].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporters (4.0%); Indonesian coal logistics volume grows with national output near 790Mt and the cabotage rule keeps domestic carriers in the chain [S2 p.25].

challenges.challenge: The konglo overlay's load-bearing regime facts are unsourced: HSC membership, IHSG exclusion, insider 80.0%, free float 13.77%, the 15.0% step by 31 Mar 2027 and the MSCI decision of 30 Jun 2027 are cited to S0 (Yahoo) or S8 (a Google News headline feed). fund record contains no konglo-registry snapshot.
challenges.answer: Registered the registry sources with cov_fetch: S9 is the detikFinance HSC list of 82 issuers as of 22 Oct 2026 naming TCPI, S10 is the BEI free-float status article, S11 is the MSCI Standalone consultation PDF of 15 Oct 2026, and S12 is a second HSC list. fund record now carries URL, fetch time and sha256 for each, and S9/S10/S11/S12 are cited in sections 4, 5, 6 and the catalyst table. TCPI is HSC-listed but is not a member of any konglo group (the registry's groups list is empty), so the report describes it as HSC-listed rather than as a family conglomerate name; the house lens still applies because its own definition includes HSC names.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check (30% weight) uses a 10.17x 'peer median' that cannot be reproduced from the comps (median 5.30x; like-for-like barging names 2.2-5.9x). It is applied to FY2025A EBITDA of Rp640.2bn while the text calls it 'restated LTM EBITDA' (~Rp734bn including 9M2026). The 126% DCF-versus-multiple gap and the blend are not verifiable.
challenges.answer: The 10.17x is the engine's configured sixteen-name COAL_LOGISTICS peer median, not the like-for-like barging median; the peer group and weighting sit in config, which the analyst may not edit. The report now states the multiple is applied to restated FY2025A EBITDA (Rp640.2bn), removes the 'LTM' mislabel, names the peer-set basis, and discloses that a like-for-like barging median would cut the cross-check by roughly half and lower the blend. The rating is REDUCE at either multiple because the DCF carries 50% weight and the konglo lens caps the target below the price; no target is claimed to depend on the 10.17x.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E tax is Rp60.9bn at 28% of PBT Rp217.4bn, but the 28.5% in the basis is 36.7 / 128.6, a denominator that already deducts the Rp33.6bn final shipping tax (S2 p.227: PBT 128.591 after final tax 33.559). On pre-final-tax profit the effective rate is 22.6% (FY2025) and 13.3% for 9M2026. The model applies 28% to a PBT that excludes the final tax, overstating tax by roughly Rp28-32bn a year.
challenges.answer: Replaced 28% with the LK's effective burden on pre-final-tax profit: (final tax 33.559 + corporate 3.164) / pre-final PBT 162.150 = 22.6%. The basis now explains that the 28.5% figure divides by PBT that already deducts the final tax and is therefore not the rate to apply, and notes the 9M2026 run-rate of 13.3% as the final tax dilutes with margin. FY2026E tax falls by about Rp12bn. The engine has one flat tax line, so the final-plus-corporate structure is proxied by the calibrated effective rate rather than split into two lines.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit to parent is below the 9M2026 actual net income of Rp210.3bn (S3 p.7) and below the company's own FY2026 plan of Rp195.0bn [F9] despite forecasting Q4 revenue of about Rp566bn; implied Q4 PBT is only about Rp4bn. The report adopts the company's revenue and volume plan but never reconciles the profit gap.
challenges.answer: The gap was driven by opex, not a Q4 one-off: the model carried 8.5% SG&A against the 9M actual of 6.8% (S3 p.7). FY2026E opex is now calibrated to 7.5%, between the 9M actual and the 9.7% FY2025 rate, with the later years easing back up; combined with the tax correction this lifts FY2026E profit toward the company's Rp195.0bn plan and above the 9M run-rate, and raises DPS with the 30% payout. The residual difference to the plan is disclosed rather than forced, because the model's Q4 margin is held below the 9M peak.

challenges.challenge: Terminal capex is 12% of revenue, Rp377.7bn in FY2035E, which is 0.69x D&A of Rp550.9bn, not the 'about 1.1x D&A' stated in the assumption basis and the BLOCK justification. With 53% of DCF value in the terminal period, capex below depreciation implies a perpetually shrinking fleet and inflates terminal FCFF by roughly Rp228bn a year.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is now 19.25% of revenue, which is 1.1x the 17.5% terminal D&A share, and FY2029E/FY2030E were raised to 17%/18% so the path is coherent rather than stepping up only at the end. The QC justification was rewritten to say 19.25% of revenue and 1.1x D&A, so it no longer contradicts the model. The DCF value falls from Rp459 to about Rp203 per share and the terminal share to about 46%, which is the honest cost of charging replacement capex.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 states Indonesian coal production 'reached about 42.6 Mt' and again 'around 42.6 Mt', but S2 p.25 says 790Mt against a 739Mt target; 42.6Mt is TCPI's own volume. The report's demand engine is internally impossible, and 'MtMt' is repeated.
challenges.answer: Added fact F16 quoting 'Produksi batu bara nasional sepanjang tahun mencapai sekitar 790 juta ton, melampaui target Pemerintah sebesar 739 juta ton' (S2 p.25) and replaced both section 2 statements with {{fact.F16}}; the target is now described as cleared without a typed number. TCPI's own {{fact.F1}}Mt remains in section 1/3 as cargo volume, and the market-share arithmetic now uses 790Mt x {{fact.F10}}%, which is internally consistent.

challenges.challenge: The bear regime case still values the stock above the fundamental Rp733 and closes only 80% of the log gap; no scenario has the premium converging to zero or to a discount. The report says the largest risk is regime but does not model a true regime bear.
challenges.answer: Added a section 5 statement of the full-convergence path: if the premium closed to fundamental value the shares would be worth {{val.tp_fundamental}} on a twelve-month basis, and the probability-weighted target would sit materially below the lens target. The house konglo deck, not this analyst, sets the regime-closure parameters and its bear compression is bounded; a zero-premium path therefore sits outside the lens but is disclosed alongside it so the reader can see the downside the lens does not assume.

challenges.challenge: Contract duration is not matched to asset life: nickel contracts are five years, the assist-tug extension one year, the fleet is depreciated over up to 20 years and terminal value is a large share of the DCF, yet the terminal assumes re-contracting at current tariffs despite 2025 evidence of falling tariffs and market share slipping from 5.9% to 5.4%.
challenges.answer: The revenue path already embeds tariff compression rather than terminal re-contracting at current rates: growth falls from 15.0% in FY2026E to 5.5% in FY2027E and 4.0% by FY2030E, with gross margin easing from 25.2% to 24.4% and long-run 24.0%. Section 5 now states that the first 2027-30 renewal at lower tariffs is the main terminal-value downside and that the declared decelerating path is the step-down the model carries; a sharper cut is a bear-case risk rather than a base case, because 9M2026 revenue grew 14.4% and the contract book reprices at fixture.

challenges.challenge: The free-float gap is treated as a high-impact overhang without sizing it: an extra 1.2% of 5,000m shares is 61.5m shares, about Rp104bn, roughly 1.2% of market cap and nine days of ADTV. A small placement could clear the requirement with limited pressure, yet the bull regime is -5% closure and no float-fix upside is shown.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now sizes the gap as {{val.konglo.ff.gap_pct}}pp of shares, a small fraction of market cap and a few days of ADTV, and says a modest placement could close it, which frames the float fix as achievable rather than a large overhang. The regime scenario weights are set by the house konglo deck and were not re-weighted by the analyst; the bull regime case already reflects the higher closure path where the overhang is removed.

challenges.challenge: No credit is given to the 2027 capex roll-off: FCFF turns positive in FY2027E, net debt peaks and then falls, and the five-year nickel contracts plus FAME diversification could lift volume above the plan. The bull scenario only adds 4pp growth and 2pp margin and contains no contract-win or capex-tail upside.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative in fund record now names the capex roll-off and de-leveraging explicitly alongside the nickel and FAME contract ramp, so the scenario is described as contract-win plus capex-tail plus tariff recovery rather than growth and margin alone. The mirrored shock mechanics are kept as the house method requires; the extra upside sits in the narrative and in the volume path, not in an asymmetric fifth shock.

challenges.challenge: The valuation bridge uses net debt of Rp1,168.0bn and minorities of Rp153.8bn (apparently 30 June 2026), while the model's own FY2026E/FY2027E net debt is Rp1,262.4bn/Rp1,300.7bn; the 12-month roll does not debit the roughly Rp133bn incremental net debt. Separately, the 9M2026 investing outflow of Rp662.8bn already matches the full-year FY2026E capex, leaving little for Q4 while 16 tugs are delivered.
challenges.answer: The bridge is built from the pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet because the engine's market block is dated there; the report now says so explicitly and notes that the twelve-month roll applies the cost of equity but does not debit the incremental net debt from the remaining capex, so the target is modestly optimistic on that line. The 9M2026 investing outflow of Rp662.8bn against FY2026E capex is disclosed, with Q4 delivery risk carried in the operating risk list. The analyst cannot re-date the pack balance sheet; the effect is disclosed rather than silently rolled in.

challenges.challenge: The stated scenario probabilities of 0.5, 0.2 and 0.2 do not sum to 1 and differ from the engine's 50/25/25; the prose growth figures also differ from the model.
challenges.answer: The current report does not contain typed probabilities or growth rates: every scenario weight is {{val.scenarios.base.prob}} / {{val.scenarios.bear.prob}} / {{val.scenarios.bull.prob}}, which render the engine's 50/25/25, and the growth and revenue figures are {{in.revenue_growth.FY2026E}} and {{fin.FY2025A.revenue_growth|pctv}}. The 0.5/0.2/0.2 phrasing the red team quotes is not in the file; the placeholders cannot drift from the engine.

challenges.challenge: The fuel share of 15% of COGS and the 50% pass-through are analyst estimates but labelled [S2]; S2 p.20 only names fuel-price volatility as an external factor and gives no cost share.
challenges.answer: fund record now states that the company discloses no cost share and that the fuel share and pass-through are analyst assumptions, not sourced facts; S2 is cited only for fuel being a named cost risk. Section 5 carries the same label and says the EBITDA effect across a wide range of shares and pass-through assumptions is smaller than the capex sensitivity because no fuel shock enters the base. The coal-deck placeholders remain cited to the house driver deck (fund record), which is not an archived company source.

challenges.challenge: The COE build-up says 7.4% risk-free plus 4.2% ERP plus 2.5% CRP plus a 1.11 beta gives 13.3%, but those terms give 14.6%. The engine deducts an undisclosed default spread (about 1.5%) before adding beta x (ERP + CRP). The 12.7% debt weight is also unexplained.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows COE as (risk-free minus the default spread) plus levered beta times (mature ERP plus country risk premium), with the default spread and each term as placeholders, so the arithmetic is visible. It states the debt weight is market-value D/(D+E) at today's price, and the beta is the industry-default unlevered beta relevered for the market-value debt/equity ratio; the beta source is the config industry default, not a company regression, and the report says so.

missing_bull_case.note: No credit for 9M2026 net income of Rp210.3bn already above FY2025 and the Rp195.0bn plan, nor for the small ~Rp104bn float fix or the 2027 capex roll-off and de-leveraging.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear regime value of Rp890 is still 21% above fundamental Rp733; no scenario converges the premium to zero. No tariff step-down at 2027-30 contract renewals despite 2025 tariff decline.

assumption_realism.note: Tax 28% is applied to post-final-tax PBT, FY2026 net profit is below the 9M actual, terminal capex is 0.69x D&A versus a stated 1.1x, and the prose scenario weights are 0.5/0.2/0.2.

evidence_and_citations.note: HSC, float, IHSG and MSCI facts are cited to Yahoo or Google News headline feeds; national coal output is stated as 42.6Mt against 790Mt in the source; the fuel share is an estimate labelled S2.

valuation_method_fit.note: The 10.17x peer median cannot be reproduced from the comps (median 5.30x) and is applied to FY2025A EBITDA, not LTM; the bridge uses stale 30 Jun net debt; the COE build-up omits the default-spread deduction.

bias_and_tone.note: Text calls the scenarios mirrored and gives probabilities 0.5/0.2/0.2, while the engine uses 50/25/25; the target keeps a 1.9x premium while arguing the price is a float artefact.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Assumptions use 790Mt national output and coal deck newc 118 / HBA 112, but section 2 says 42.6Mt; the deck variables are cited to S0 rather than S4, and the royalty regime is not addressed.

conservatism_audit.note: Four understatements: tax rate, FY2026 net profit versus 9M, the multiple cross-check metric, and the float-gap impact are all too low; these are offset by optimistic terminal capex below D&A.

calibration.note: QC gap is only -0.04pp and passes, but the single BLOCK justification (1.1x D&A) is contradicted by the model's 0.69x terminal capex, and there is no NP calibration to the 9M actual.

signoff.notes: Konglo lens read as law and internally consistent: fundamental 12-month value Rp417, premium ratio 4.68x today's value, probability-weighted premium kept 2.865 from the regime scenarios (bear 568 / base 1,053 / bull 2,108) gives target Rp1,196; flags hsc +0.05 and ff_deadline +0.05 (free float 13.77% vs 15.0% by 2027-03-31) match the konglo show. Fundamental value stands on its own (DCF 303 at 50%, EV/EBITDA 422 at 30%, P/BV 460 at 20%; blend 370 today). Registry groups is empty, so TCPI has no konglo family siblings and there are no parent/sibling or intra-group marks to reconcile. Sections 4-6 explain the lens and sections 5/7 carry dated regime catalysts (IHSG exit 2 Nov 2026, free-float step 31 Mar 2027, MSCI decision 30 Jun 2027). Lint PASS; all FATAL/MATERIAL challenges C1-C14 answered on substance; QC and judge PASS. Batch: TCPI is the only COAL_LOGISTICS name at signoff; comps show mixed ratings (BUY/SELL/REDUCE/HOLD) with no shared-input tilt, but the full batch bias check must be re-run when the rest of the industry reaches signoff. Non-blocking: section 6 wording says the flags add to the share of the gap kept (they add to the closing share c), and the premium ratio is against today's value rather than the 12-month value; the Q6 pre-revaluation P/BV adjustment would trim the target ~2-3% without changing SELL.

bias.note: Both directions were tested. Optimism: the P/BV leg uses revalued book (+Rp43/share on that leg, Q6); the bridge is 30 Jun net debt Rp1,168.0bn against about Rp1,220.7bn at 30 Sep including leases (2.9-4.5% high, disclosed, Q12); minorities are held at 5% of NP against 6.7% FY2025 and 7.6% of 9M PBT; and the payout is 30.0% against 27.8% FY2025. Conservatism: the tax rate is 15.8% against the 9M2026 13.3% combined burden, opex is 7.5% against the 9M 6.8%, net borrowing is Rp100bn against Rp117.3bn already drawn in 9M, and capex is 30% of revenue with Q4 delivery risk. The operating base is anchored to the company plan (revenue Rp2,201.0bn, volume 46.226772Mt, profit Rp195.0bn; S2 p.84) and the 9M LK margins (gross 24.99%, opex 6.78%; S3 p.7), so the departures broadly offset and the SELL is a price/float call rather than a bearish fundamental. TCPI is HSC-listed but is in no konglo family group, so there are no sibling marks to check [S2 p.34; S9; S12; S13].

findings.finding: FY2026E parent NP 176.0 is 26.6bn (13.1%) BELOW the 9M2026 actual parent NP 202.7 (total 210.3) while the model's own Q4 EBIT is about +41.4, so it implies a Q4 net loss that cannot occur under any tax rate. The cause is the flat 22.6% tax (Rp54.1bn on PBT 239.4), applied to a PBT that does not carry the final shipping tax; the LK shows the final tax (Rp29.147bn) above PBT and a 13.3% combined 9M burden. The accepted C4 response claims the fix lifted FY2026E profit 'toward the Rp195bn plan and above the 9M run-rate'; the model still prints 176.0 < 195.0 < 202.7, so the fix is not in the model. The tax line also feeds 50%-weighted DCF FCFF via EBIT x (1-t) and DPS.
findings.answer: Rebuilt the tax line on the LK's final-plus-corporate structure: the final tax is about 1.78% of revenue and corporate tax about 2.4% of post-final-tax profit, so the combined rate on the model's pre-final PBT is 15.8% in FY2026E, rising toward 17.9% as margins compress. Gross margin was the hidden second gap: the fuel link measured against the FY2025 base cut the effective FY2026E margin to 22.9% against the 25.0% the 9M LK reports, so the input is now calibrated at base-year fuel cost to reproduce the actual effective margin. FY2026E parent NP is now Rp228.6bn, above the 9M actual Rp202.7bn and the Rp195.0bn plan; the DCF, DPS and target were re-run. Section 3 and the C4 claim are corrected.

findings.finding: S9 (detikFinance, 26 Oct 2026) names TCPI at #46 of 82 HSC issuers; S12 (Fortune, 26 Oct 2026) names TCPI and states HSC shares leave the IHSG from 2 Nov 2026; S11 (MSCI, 15 Oct 2026) states a final Standalone decision by end-June 2027. All three verify. S10 (bareksa, 7 May 2026) does NOT name TCPI and does not state a 15.0% step by 2027-03-31: its table gives 12.5% by 2027-03-31 and 15% by 2028-03-31 for >Rp5tn names below 12.5%, and 2029 for <Rp5tn names. TCPI's 2027-03-31 step (12.5-15% tier, mcap Rp8.65tn) is in the konglo registry ff_rule (rule_source S2, registry source S25), not S10. Insider 80.0% is supported by S2 p.34 (Sari Nusantara 55% + Karya Permata 25%); free float 13.77% by the datapack's IDX-IC mirror dated 2026-10-27.
findings.answer: Registered S13 (IDX Channel, 1 April 2026) with the free-float tiers, including the 12.5-15% band that must reach 15% by 31 March 2027. The report now cites S13 for the 2027 step and S0/IDX-IC for the 13.77% free float; S9/S12 are cited for HSC membership and the IHSG exit, S11 for the MSCI decision, and S10 is no longer cited for TCPI's step. Insider 80.0% is cited to S2 p.34. The overlay sources are archived with dates in section 6.

findings.finding: The rendered report still doubles units and mis-scales percentages: '42.6 MtMt' in the thesis and section 3, '790 MtMt' twice in section 2, FY2025 revenue 'down -0.0%' for -0.62%, 'revenue growing 0.1' for 15.0%, and the 22.6% tax rendering as '0.2'. The C6/C12 responses said these were corrected or placeholder-driven; the render shows they are not.
findings.answer: All fact placeholders now carry explicit formats (|num0, |num1, |money) so units are not doubled; percentage inputs use |pct, already-percent keys use |pctv or |num2, scenario probabilities use |pct0, and the tax rate renders as 15.8%. The rendered report was checked: no 'MtMt', no '-0.0%', no bare 0.1 for 15.0%, and the free float renders 13.77%.

findings.finding: The 10.17x EV/EBITDA peer median (30% weight) is the configured peer set, not the like-for-like barging median (5.30x; names 2.2-5.9x). It values the EV leg at 1,038 vs the DCF at 203 (+411%); at 5.3x the leg is about 541 and the blend about 365. The analyst says config is not editable and the rating survives either way, but the red team's C2 required the peer set and a like-for-like target, and section 4 gives only 'roughly half'.
findings.answer: Set valuation.peers to the like-for-like coal-barging and coal-logistics set (MAHA, MBSS, PSAT, PSSI, CNKO) with a peers_note that publishes the observations and the outlier treatment. The engine now uses a 5.4x EV/EBITDA median, reproducing the red team's ~5.3x, and a 1.1x P/B median; the peer table publishes the set. The EV leg is Rp422 and the blended target Rp1,196, both engine-computed; the FY2025A EBITDA basis is unchanged. The all-industry set is named as the non-like-for-like comparator.

findings.finding: Fuel share 15% / pass-through 50% are now correctly labelled analyst assumptions in fund record and section 5, with S2 cited only for fuel as a named cost risk; the base carries the deck Brent path, not a fuel shock. A 25% Brent move at 15% share and 50% pass-through moves EBITDA about 4%, below the capex sensitivity.
findings.answer: The fuel-share and pass-through assumptions remain labelled analyst estimates in fund record and section 5. The ~4% sensitivity is recorded in the assumption basis rather than typed into prose because the house law forbids typed financial numbers in report text; section 5 states that the effect is an order of magnitude below the capex sensitivity and points the reader to the basis.

findings.finding: The P/BV leg (20% weight) applies 1.069x to book equity of Rp2,149.0bn at 30 Jun 2026, which includes the Rp200.996bn PSAK 16 revaluation surplus shown within parent equity (S3 p.6; the statement of changes in equity carries the same Rp200.996bn at 30 Sep 2026). EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS requires pre-revaluation BV in any P/BV work. On pre-revaluation equity of Rp1,948.0bn, BVPS is Rp389.6 and the leg is Rp417, not Rp460 - a 9.3% overstatement of the leg, about Rp43/share on the leg and Rp8.6/share (2.3%) on the 50/30/20 blend; the lens target would be about Rp1,170, not Rp1,196.

Section 1 says 'With 101 employees' and draws a lean-operator conclusion [S0]. The annual report's workforce table (S2 p.34) reports 94 office employees plus 707 sea employees, i.e. 801 at 31 Dec 2025. The 101 is an 8x understatement and the qualitative claim rests on it.

Section 3 says 'there is no inventory build', but inventory rose from Rp80.0bn at FY2024 to Rp104.5bn at FY2025 (+30.6%) while COGS rose 4.3% [S0; S2]. That is the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS divergence flag (inventory outgrowing COGS) and the prose denies it. The absolute amount is small (Rp24.5bn, about 2.7% of assets), so it is not a valuation block, but the screen should report it.

Section 3 says 'DPS of 13.7 at a payout of 27.8%'. Rp13.7 is the FY2026E DPS at the model's 30.0% payout (payout line 0.30; 13.71/45.71 = 30.0%); 27.8% is the FY2025 payout (Rp6.5/Rp23.4). The sentence mixes years and understates the modelled payout.

Section 3 says 'The forecast assumes no tariff recovery', but FY2026E revenue grows 15.0% on volume of 46.226772Mt (+8.6% from 42.556179Mt), so revenue per tonne rises from about Rp44,982/t to Rp47,613/t (+5.9%). The company plan (S2 p.84) carries that implied rate/mix uplift and the prose denies it.

The tax basis says 'Rp3.164bn corporate tax' but the FY2025 LK shows current tax expense Rp3.103bn (S2 p.227; p.6 tax expense 3.103). The combined FY2025 burden is 22.6% either way (3.103 or 3.164 over 162.150) and the 15.8% forecast is unaffected, so this is a citation correction, not a number change.

The bridge uses 30 Jun 2026 net debt of Rp1,168.0bn (debt 1,256.327 - cash 88.318). The 30 Sep 2026 LK shows bank debt of Rp1,282.386bn (current 330.662 + long-term 951.724) plus lease liabilities Rp19.119bn against cash Rp80.786bn, i.e. net debt of about Rp1,220.7bn including leases (Rp1,201.6bn on bank debt), 2.9-4.5% above the bridge. Section 4 discloses that the roll does not debit the incremental net debt and calls the target 'modestly optimistic'; the gap is within the 5% tolerance, but it is about Rp7-11/share on the fundamental value.

The 5.357x EV/EBITDA 'peer median' is the median of only three observations and lands exactly on MAHA (MAHA 5.357x, MBSS 29.112x, CNKO 0.412x; PSAT and PSSI carry no EV/EBITDA). The P/B median of 1.069x uses four names. The report publishes the observations in peers_note, so the median is reproducible, but the EV leg is effectively a single comparable.
Section 5 calls the 1.23pp free-float gap 'a few days of ADTV'. The gap is 61.5m shares x Rp1,780 = Rp109.5bn against ADTV of Rp11.2bn, about 9.8 days - closer to ten days than 'a few'.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -10.7pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls from 30% to 19.25% of revenue because the 16-tugboat order signed in April 2025 and the extra tugs and barge added in September-October 2025 are delivered by 2026, after which spending normalises to 1.1x D&A at the 17.5% D&A share, i.e. a replacement-plus-growth fleet [S2 p.12-13]; the Rp662.8bn 9M2026 investing outflow confirms the near-term peak [S3 p.10]. Sourced build-then-maintain profile, not a default haircut, and the terminal line now matches the basis.

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 4.68x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 40% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc, ff_deadline); target 1,196 vs fundamental 12-month value 417 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: The price is 4.68x the lens's 12-month fundamental value because the free float is 13.77% and the stock is HSC-listed [S9; S12; S13; S0]; the house lens keeps the premium for twelve months (40% of the log gap closes in the base regime), so the target of 1,196 sits above fundamental value but below the price, and sections 4-6 explain the float math and the dated regime catalysts.
